High doses of methenamine (8 grams daily for 3 to 4 weeks) have been associated with bladder irritation, painful and frequent urination, the presence of albumin in the urine (albuminuria), and visible blood in the urine (gross hematuria). 2. Methenamine hippurate tablets should not be prescribed in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication, as this is unlikely to benefit the patient and may increase the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 3. It is important to maintain an acidic pH in the urine, particularly when treating infections caused by urea-splitting organisms such as Proteus species and certain strains of Pseudomonas. 4. In a limited number of cases from one study, serum transaminase levels were slightly elevated during treatment with methenamine hippurate tablets but returned to normal while the patients continued taking the medication. 5. Based on this observation, it is recommended to periodically monitor liver function in patients taking methenamine hippurate, especially those with pre-existing liver dysfunction. 6. The safety of methenamine hippurate tablets during early pregnancy has not been established. In the last trimester, safety is suggested but not definitively proven. 7. Studies in pregnant rats and rabbits did not show adverse effects on the fetus. However, methenamine hippurate tablets taken during pregnancy can interfere with laboratory tests measuring urinary estriol when acid hydrolysis is used, leading to unmeasurably low values. This interference is due to the presence of methenamine and/or formaldehyde in the urine. Using enzymatic hydrolysis instead of acid hydrolysis can avoid this issue. 8. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including methenamine hippurate tablets, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). 9. When prescribed for a bacterial infection, patients should be advised to take methenamine hippurate tablets exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of treatment may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance, making them untreatable with methenamine hippurate or other antibacterial drugs in the future. 10. Clinical studies of methenamine hippurate did not include enough subjects aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. 11. In general, dosing for elderly patients should be cautious, typically starting at the lower end of the dosing range. This approach reflects the higher likelihood of reduced liver, kidney, or heart function, as well as the presence of other diseases or concurrent drug therapies in this population.
